title: What a kernel does: system calls and user mode
goal: By the end you can explain how a program crosses from user mode into the kernel and back, read strace output, and say why some calls never show up in it.

warmup.q: A Java program does one thing: `System.out.println("hello")`. On Linux, about how many system calls does the JVM make from start to exit?
options: One: a single `write`
About 30, like any small program
About 1,400
About 100,000, one per bytecode it runs
warmup.why: In the lab box a Java hello world makes about 1,440 system calls. A C program that prints the same line makes 28. The JVM spends its calls mapping memory (`mmap`, `mprotect`), starting about 20 threads and making them wait for each other (`futex`). The `println` itself is one `write`. Bytecode runs in user mode and needs no system call at all.

sections.h: Programs can't touch the hardware, so they ask the kernel
sections.body:
Right now the lab box's Linux runs your shell, a JVM and a dozen other programs on the same CPUs, the same memory and the same disk. Picture what happens if each program drives that hardware itself. The payment service writes a ledger block to the SSD while a log shipper writes to the same spot. A bug in one program overwrites another program's memory, including the memory that holds a card-issuer API key. A program stuck in an endless loop keeps a CPU forever. Nobody is in charge, so nothing stops any of it.

The first fix you might try is a shared library: every program calls the same careful disk and memory code. That doesn't help. Library code runs with exactly the powers of the program that called it, so a buggy or hostile program can skip the library and poke the hardware directly.

So the protection has to come from the CPU itself. A CPU has two modes. In **kernel mode** it runs every instruction. In **user mode** it refuses the privileged ones: the instructions that talk to devices or switch which memory a program can see. If user-mode code tries one, the CPU stops it on the spot. arm64, the CPU family in an Apple Silicon Mac and in the lab box, calls the two modes EL1 and EL0. x86-64 calls them ring 0 and ring 3.

Now no program in user mode can hurt another. It also can't do anything useful, such as reading a file. The last piece is a controlled door. The **kernel** is the one program that runs in kernel mode. It owns the CPUs, the memory, the disks and the network card, and it decides which program runs next. Every other program is a user program: your JVM, bash, PostgreSQL, even the Docker daemon. A user program that needs something asks the kernel with a **system call**, a request with a number that names the service: `openat` (open a file), `read`, `write`, `mmap` (give me memory), `clone` (start a new thread or process). The kernel checks the request, does the work and hands back a result. Linux has a few hundred of them. On arm64, `write` is number 64.

The endless loop needs one more thing. Before the kernel lets a program run, it arms a hardware timer. On the lab box's kernel the timer fires about every millisecond. Each time, the CPU stops the program and jumps into the kernel (this is a timer interrupt), and the kernel can then pick another program to run. Lesson 4 of this track is about that choice.

That is the picture for this whole track, drawn below. Programs sit on top in user mode, the hardware sits at the bottom, the kernel sits in between, and system calls are the only way through. Each later lesson opens up one box of the kernel.

sections.h: A Java hello world makes about 1,400 system calls
sections.body:
`strace` lets you watch the requests go by. It stops a program at every system call, prints the call with its arguments and its result, and lets the program carry on. (It does this through `ptrace`, the kernel's debugging interface, which is also what debuggers use.) `-c` prints a count per call instead of every line, and `-f` also follows every thread and child process the program starts. A **thread** is one line of execution inside a program, with its own place in the code. A JVM runs many at once, and lesson 3 of this track looks at them closely.

Here is what three programs that do almost nothing ask for, counted in the lab box:

```text
/bin/true                 26 system calls
C hello world             28
Java hello world       1,440
```

`/bin/true` does nothing and exits, and it still needs 26 calls just to start: load the C library (libc, the library almost every Linux program uses to make its system calls), set up memory, then exit. The C program adds a `write` and little else. The JVM's top calls show where its 1,440 go: `mmap` 275 times, to reserve memory for its heap and load its libraries; `futex` 258 times, which is one thread waiting for another or waking it; and `mprotect` 219 times, to change what a range of memory may be used for. The one `write` that prints your line is near the bottom of the list.

Those calls buy a garbage-collected heap, a JIT compiler and about 20 threads, all set up before your `main` runs, and each step needs the kernel. The Try-it below gets you the same numbers.

try.title: Count system calls for three programs
steps: From the `labs` folder on your Mac, start the lab box: `docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box`. You land in `/labs`. strace is Linux only. macOS has `dtruss`, but System Integrity Protection blocks it for most programs, so run this track's Try-its in the box.
Predict the three totals before you run anything.

Run the commands below. The first three print one total line each. The last line prints the JVM's top five calls and its total. The C program is `os/c/l01/hello.c` and the Java one is `os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l01/demo/Hello.java`.

code.title: in the lab box
code.src:
strace -c /bin/true 2>&1 | tail -1
gcc -O2 -o /tmp/hello os/c/l01/hello.c
strace -c /tmp/hello 2>&1 | tail -1
gcc -O2 -static -o /tmp/hello-static os/c/l01/hello.c
strace -c /tmp/hello-static 2>&1 | tail -1
javac -d /tmp/out os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l01/demo/*.java
strace -f -c -S calls -o /tmp/jc.txt java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l01.demo.Hello 2>/dev/null
head -7 /tmp/jc.txt; tail -1 /tmp/jc.txt

try.expect:
Totals of about 26, 28, 14 and 1,440. They move by a few calls between runs:

```text
100.00    0.000083           3        26         1 total
100.00    0.000000           0        28         1 total
100.00    0.000000           0        14           total
hello from the JVM
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ------------------
  1.18    0.001250           4       275           mmap
 91.87    0.097266         377       258        34 futex
  1.15    0.001219           5       219           mprotect
  0.98    0.001036           7       141           rt_sigprocmask
  0.30    0.000313           4        66        17 openat
100.00    0.105870          73      1440        77 total
```

The static C binary has the C library built in, so it needs no dynamic loader (the code that finds and maps shared libraries such as `libc.so.6` before `main` runs) and makes half as many calls. Most entries in the `errors` column are normal: the loader and the JVM look for files in several places and get `ENOENT` until they find the right one.

sections.h: A system call is a trap into kernel mode and back
sections.body:
Asking the kernel can't be an ordinary function call. If a program could jump to any address inside the kernel, it could land just past the code that checks permissions and run the rest with full power. So the CPU offers one special instruction that does three things at once: it switches to kernel mode, it saves where the program was, and it jumps to an entry point the kernel chose at boot. The program can't choose where it lands. This switch is called a **trap**. On arm64 the instruction is `svc` (supervisor call). On x86-64 it is `syscall`.

With one entry point for everything, the kernel needs to be told which service you want and with which inputs. Both travel in **registers**, the few dozen small storage slots inside the CPU that instructions work on directly. arm64 has 31 general ones, named `x0` to `x30`. The service is a number, the system call number, and the kernel looks it up in a table.

Here is `write(1, "ok\n", 3)`, which asks the kernel to write 3 bytes to file descriptor 1. A **file descriptor** is a small number a program uses to name something it has open. 0 is standard input, 1 is standard output (usually your terminal) and 2 is standard error.

1. Your code calls the C library's `write` function. That part is an ordinary function call, still in user mode.
2. The library's wrapper puts the system call number, 64, in register `x8` and the three arguments in `x0`, `x1` and `x2`.
3. It runs `svc #0`. The CPU traps: it saves the program counter (the address of the next instruction to run), switches from EL0 to EL1 and jumps to the kernel's entry point.
4. The kernel reads `x8`, looks up entry 64 in its system call table and runs the write handler. The handler checks that file descriptor 1 is open for writing and copies the 3 bytes out of your memory.
5. The kernel puts the result in `x0` and runs `eret`, which switches back to user mode at the instruction right after `svc`.

Step 4 has a detail worth a second look. The kernel checks the buffer's address before it copies. A program could pass the address of kernel memory as its "buffer" and ask the kernel to write the kernel's own secrets to a file. The check stops that, so the kernel never trusts a pointer that comes from user mode.

Errors come back as negative numbers. If a file is missing, `openat` puts -2 in `x0`. The C library turns that into a return value of -1 and sets a variable called `errno` to 2, which has the name `ENOENT` (no such file or directory). strace shows both at once: `= -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)`. Java turns the same failure into a `NoSuchFileException`.

The round trip costs time. In the lab box one `getpid` system call takes about 150 ns, measured in the last Try-it of this lesson. That is nothing once and a lot a million times. Code that makes one system call per tiny piece of work, like a logger that writes every line straight to its file or a reader that pulls one byte at a time from a socket, pays the 150 ns on every piece.

try.title: Watch a call succeed, then fail
steps: In the box, trace only `openat`, `read` and `write` while `cat` prints one file that exists and one that doesn't.
Find the two `openat` lines for `/etc/hostname` and `/etc/nope`. Compare what each returned.
try.expect:
strace's lines and `cat`'s own output both go to the terminal, so they mix. Output trimmed to the interesting part:

```text
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/hostname", O_RDONLY) = 3
read(3, "box\n", 131072)                = 4
box
write(1, "box\n", 4)                    = 4
read(3, "", 131072)                     = 0
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/nope", O_RDONLY) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
write(2, "cat: ", 5cat: )                    = 5
write(2, "/etc/nope", 9/etc/nope)                = 9
...
+++ exited with 1 +++
```

The first `openat` returns file descriptor 3, a small number that names the open file in the `read` calls after it. A `read` that returns 0 means end of file. The second `openat` returns -1 with `ENOENT`, so `cat` writes its complaint to fd 2 (standard error) and exits with status 1. There is no `open` call anywhere: arm64 Linux only has `openat`. Tutorials written on x86 machines may show `open`, `fork` or `stat`. On arm64 you see `openat`, `clone` and `newfstatat` instead.

sections.h: What the JVM asks the kernel for before main runs
sections.body:
Save a full trace of the Java hello world to a file and read it from the top. The first number on each line is the **TID**, the thread ID: a number the kernel gives every thread. These lines come from one run in the lab box (long lines trimmed):

```text
143   execve("/opt/java/openjdk/bin/java", ["java", "-cp", "/tmp/out", "sfz.os.l01.demo.Hello"], 0xffffc2466180 /* 14 vars */) = 0
143   openat(AT_FDCWD, "/opt/java/openjdk/bin/libjli.so", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
143   openat(AT_FDCWD, "/opt/java/openjdk/bin/../lib/libjli.so", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = 3
143   openat(AT_FDCWD, "/opt/java/openjdk/lib/server/libjvm.so", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = 3
143   clone3({flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|..., stack_size=0x1fca60, ...}, 88) = -1 ENOSYS (Function not implemented)
143   clone(child_stack=0xffff8a94ea60, flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|..., parent_tid=[144], ...) = 144
143   futex(0xffff8a94f270, FUTEX_WAIT_BITSET|FUTEX_CLOCK_REALTIME, 144, NULL, FUTEX_BITSET_MATCH_ANY <unfinished ...>
144   write(1, "hello from the JVM\n", 19) = 19
```

`execve` loads a program into the process, here the `java` **launcher**: the small program that reads your command line and starts the JVM. The launcher needs two **shared libraries**, files of compiled code that a program loads at start-up (on Linux they end in `.so`). It looks for `libjli.so` next to itself, gets `ENOENT`, and finds it one folder up, where `openat` returns 3: the file descriptor for the now-open file. (`AT_FDCWD` means "relative to the current directory" and `O_RDONLY` means read-only.) Then it opens `libjvm.so`, which is the JVM itself.

Then comes a surprise. The launcher doesn't run your program on its own thread. It starts thread 144 with `clone` and then waits on a `futex` until 144 is done (the `144` inside that call is the thread ID it waits for). Thread 144 builds the JVM, the JVM starts 19 more threads (garbage collector, JIT compilers, a signal dispatcher and others), and 144 finally runs `main` and makes the one `write` that prints your line. Thread 143, whose ID is also the process ID, sits in that futex call until the end.

The failed `clone3` is not a JVM bug. `clone3` is the newer way to start a thread, and the C library (glibc) tries it first. Every container on a host shares one kernel, so a bug in some rarely used system call, reachable from one container, would be a way into all of them. Docker's answer is **seccomp**, a filter the kernel runs on every system call a container makes, before the call itself runs. Docker's default filter answers `clone3` with `ENOSYS`, which means "this call doesn't exist". glibc believes it and falls back to the older `clone`, which does the same job. In the privileged lab box (`box-priv`), which runs without a seccomp filter, all 20 threads start with `clone3` on the first try. The kernel is the same in both boxes, and only the filter at the door differs.

try.title: Find the JVM's threads in its trace
steps: In the box, save a full trace of the hello world to a file, then pull out the lines below. If this is a new box, run the `javac` line from the first Try-it again.
Count the `clone(` lines. Which thread wrote `hello from the JVM`: the process's own ID, or another one?

Type `exit`. Start the privileged box with `docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box-priv`, run `javac -d /tmp/out os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l01/demo/Hello.java`, run the `strace -f -o` line again, then `grep -c 'clone3(' /tmp/t.txt` and `grep -c 'clone(' /tmp/t.txt`.

code.title: in the lab box
code.src:
strace -f -o /tmp/t.txt java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l01.demo.Hello
head -1 /tmp/t.txt
grep clone3 /tmp/t.txt
grep -c 'clone(' /tmp/t.txt
grep 'write(1' /tmp/t.txt

try.expect:
Thread IDs change on every run. Long lines trimmed:

```text
hello from the JVM
98    execve("/opt/java/openjdk/bin/java", ["java", "-cp", "/tmp/out", "sfz.os.l01.demo.Hello"], 0xffffda7a6fd0 /* 14 vars */) = 0
98    clone3({flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|...}, 88) = -1 ENOSYS (Function not implemented)
20
99    write(1, "hello from the JVM\n", 19) = 19
```

One failed `clone3`, then 20 thread starts with `clone`. The line was written by thread 99, the one the launcher started, not by 98, the process ID. In `box-priv` the two counts flip to 20 and 0: every thread starts with `clone3`, because nothing filters it.

sections.h: Some calls never reach the kernel: the vDSO
sections.body:
`System.nanoTime()` reads a clock, and on Linux reading a clock means the `clock_gettime` system call. A service that times every request reads the clock millions of times. At about 150 ns per trap, that adds up to real CPU. Yet the time is only a number the kernel already knows, so trapping into the kernel to read it is a lot of ceremony.

The simplest fix: the kernel writes the current time into a page of memory that every process can read. A **page** is the unit the kernel hands out memory in, 4 KB in the lab box. Reading a number from memory takes a nanosecond or two. That version has two problems. The kernel updates the page while you might be reading it, so you could get half an old value and half a new one. And the raw value is a count of hardware clock ticks that has to be converted to nanoseconds, with factors the kernel adjusts as it corrects the clock.

So the kernel maps two things into every process it starts: the data page, and a small piece of code that knows how to read it. The code checks a counter that the kernel bumps on every update, and reads again if an update was in progress. Then it converts the ticks to nanoseconds. Code plus data, already in your process: that is the **vDSO** (virtual dynamic shared object). When you call `clock_gettime`, the C library calls the vDSO's version and never traps. On arm64 the vDSO exports `clock_gettime`, `gettimeofday` and `clock_getres`, plus one helper the kernel uses when it delivers signals (lesson 2 of this track). Every process's memory map, the list of memory regions it may use that `/proc/self/maps` prints, shows the vDSO as two small regions: `[vdso]` for the code and `[vvar]` for the data.

The numbers from the lab box: a real system call (`getpid`) took about 150 ns and a vDSO `clock_gettime` about 17 ns. A Java loop of one million `System.nanoTime()` calls ran at about 18 ns per call.

Two things follow. First, strace can't see vDSO calls, because they never reach the kernel. A trace of that million-call loop counts 3 `clock_gettime` system calls, and all 3 come from JVM start-up reading per-thread CPU-time clocks (clocks that count how much CPU one thread has used), which the vDSO doesn't serve. If you trace a program to learn how often it reads the time, strace undercounts by a million. Second, seccomp can't filter those calls either, for the same reason.

So timing every card authorization with `System.nanoTime()` costs tens of nanoseconds on Linux. It never needs a trip into the kernel.

try.title: Time a trap, then watch the vDSO hide
steps: Predict: how many `clock_gettime` system calls will strace count for a loop that calls `System.nanoTime()` one million times?
Run the commands below in the box. `os/c/l01/cost.c` times one million `getpid` system calls against one million vDSO clock reads. `NanoLoop` is the Java loop.

code.title: in the lab box
code.src:
gcc -O2 -o /tmp/cost os/c/l01/cost.c && /tmp/cost
java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l01.demo.NanoLoop
strace -f -c -e trace=clock_gettime java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l01.demo.NanoLoop 2>&1 | grep -v attached
grep -E 'vdso|vvar' /proc/self/maps

try.expect:
```text
getpid (system call):    151.0 ns per call
clock_gettime (vDSO):     16.9 ns per call
1,000,000 nanoTime() calls in 18 ms (18 ns each), checksum 1
1,000,000 nanoTime() calls in 19 ms (19 ns each), checksum 3
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ----------------
  0.00    0.000000           0         3           clock_gettime
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ----------------
100.00    0.000000           0         3           total
ffff9bd35000-ffff9bd37000 r--p 00000000 00:00 0                          [vvar]
ffff9bd37000-ffff9bd39000 r-xp 00000000 00:00 0                          [vdso]
```

A million clock reads, and strace counted 3 system calls. Your nanoseconds depend on your Mac's CPU and on the Docker VM, so expect different numbers. The gap of about 9x between the two `cost` lines is what to look at. The addresses in the last two lines change on every run, because the kernel places the vDSO at a random address.

analogy: A system call works like the counter at a bank. You can't walk into the vault. You fill in a slip with a form number and the details, push it under the glass, and wait while the teller checks your account, does the work behind the glass and slides back a result or an error code. strace is a camera above the counter that films every slip. The vDSO is the board on the wall with today's exchange rates: you read it yourself and never join the queue. The analogy breaks on time and on who does the work. A teller takes minutes and serves other people while you wait. A system call takes about 150 ns, and the kernel runs it on your own thread, on the same CPU, in time your program was already using.
in_your_world: Everything your Quarkus payment service does with the outside world is a system call. A JDBC call to Oracle is a `write` of the request on a socket and a `read` of the reply. A Kafka consumer's poll waits on its sockets with epoll and then reads them. A log line from a synchronous appender is a `write`. When a service is slow and its CPU graphs look quiet, `strace -f -c -p <pid>` for ten seconds on a staging pod shows what it is really asking for: tens of thousands of small `write` calls point to an unbuffered logger, and a wall of `futex` calls points to threads waiting on each other. strace stops the program twice per call, so a traced service can run many times slower. Keep it to staging, or to a few seconds on one pod you can afford to slow down. Timing every authorization with `System.nanoTime()` is fine, though: that goes through the vDSO.
mistake:
Attaching strace to a running JVM without `-f`. `strace -p <pid>` attaches to one thread, the one whose ID equals the process ID. In a JVM that is the launcher thread, which only waits for the main thread to finish. You get one line and then silence:

```text
futex(0xffff8904f270, FUTEX_WAIT_BITSET|FUTEX_CLOCK_REALTIME, 67, NULL, FUTEX_BITSET_MATCH_ANY
```

People read that as "the JVM is stuck on a lock". The other 30 or so threads are busy, and strace just isn't watching them. Use `strace -f -p <pid>` to attach to every thread, or pass one thread's ID to `-p` when you already know which thread you care about.

compare.title: The same JVM start-up, with and without Docker's seccomp filter

a.label: box (Docker's default seccomp)
a.title: strace -f, lab box
a.src:
143   clone3({flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|CLONE_SYSVSEM|CLONE_SETTLS|CLONE_PARENT_SETTID|CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID, ...}, 88) = -1 ENOSYS (Function not implemented)
143   clone(child_stack=0xffff8a94ea60, flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|CLONE_SYSVSEM|CLONE_SETTLS|CLONE_PARENT_SETTID|CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID, parent_tid=[144], ...) = 144

$ grep -c 'clone3(' /tmp/t.txt
1
$ grep -c 'clone(' /tmp/t.txt
20

compare.note: Same kernel (6.12), same JDK, same program. In the default box, seccomp checks each call before the kernel runs it and answers `clone3` with `ENOSYS`, so glibc retries with `clone`. Docker does this on purpose. A seccomp filter can only look at the values in the call's registers. `clone` carries its flags in a register, so the filter can check them and refuse the flags that create namespaces. `clone3` carries its flags in a struct in memory, which the filter can't read, so Docker hides the call and lets glibc fall back. Answering `ENOSYS` matters: glibc falls back only on `ENOSYS`. Any other error would make thread creation fail.

worked.title: Read a JVM start-up from its trace

steps.say: You have `/tmp/t.txt` from `strace -f -o`. Start with its shape: how many threads appear, and how did the process begin? These are the numbers for the trace the lab uses, `hello-jvm.strace.txt`.
steps.code:
# distinct thread IDs: the process plus every thread it started
awk '{print $1}' /tmp/t.txt | sort -u | wc -l
# 21

# how the process began
head -1 /tmp/t.txt
# 143   execve("/opt/java/openjdk/bin/java", ["java", "-cp", "/tmp/out", "sfz.os.l01.demo.Hello"], ...) = 0

steps.say: Next, group the failures by errno. A long tail of failures in a healthy start-up is normal, so learn what each one usually means before you call it a problem.
steps.code:
grep -o '= -1 E[A-Z]*' /tmp/t.txt | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
#   29 = -1 EAGAIN
#   23 = -1 ENOENT
#   15 = -1 EINVAL
#    3 = -1 ENOTTY
#    1 = -1 ENOSYS
#    1 = -1 EEXIST

steps.say: All 29 `EAGAIN` come from `futex`. A futex wait gives `EAGAIN` when the lock word changed between the program's check and the call, so it returns at once and lets the thread look again. `ENOENT` is the loader and the JVM probing for files. `ENOTTY` is a terminal check on something that isn't a terminal. The single `ENOSYS` is the `clone3` that seccomp refused.

Last, the thread starts. A thread start is a `clone` or `clone3` with `CLONE_THREAD` that returned a positive number, the new thread's ID. When another thread prints in the middle of a call, strace splits the call in two lines, so the result can sit far from the flags. A `grep` for `= 145` would miss what it belongs to. That's why the lab builds a small parser that joins the halves.
steps.code:
144   clone(child_stack=0xffff890c3a60, flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|CLONE_SYSVSEM|CLONE_SETTLS|CLONE_PARENT_SETTID|CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID <unfinished ...>
145   rseq(0xffff890c48c0, 0x20, 0, 0xd428bc00 <unfinished ...>
144   <... clone resumed>, parent_tid=[145], tls=0xffff890c48e0, child_tidptr=0xffff890c4270) = 145

lab.title: Build an strace log analyzer
steps: Open `hello-jvm.strace.txt`. It is a real `strace -f -o` capture of this lesson's hello world from the lab box. Find one `<unfinished ...>` line and its `resumed` partner.
Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All ten fail with `NotImplementedError`.

Write `StraceParser.parseResult`. Split the text on whitespace. The first word is the result: `?`, a `0x` hex number or a decimal. The second word is the errno when it looks like `E` followed by capitals.

Write `StraceParser.parse`. Match `PREFIX` to get the pid and the rest of the line. Try `RESUMED`, then `UNFINISHED`, then `COMPLETE` on the rest. Keep unfinished halves in a `MutableMap<Int, Pair<String, String>>` keyed by pid, and build the `Syscall` when the resumed half arrives.
Write the four `StraceReport` methods. Each one is a `filter` followed by a `groupingBy` or a `map`.
Run the tests until all ten pass. Then read what they check against the real trace: 1,453 calls, `mmap` first, 20 threads, one `ENOSYS`, 51 files opened.
hints: `groupingBy { it.name }.eachCount()` gives a `Map<String, Int>`. Sort its entries with `sortedByDescending { it.value }` and rebuild the map with `associate { it.key to it.value }`, which keeps that order.
For hex, `removePrefix("0x").toULong(16).toLong()` handles every 64-bit value. Plain `toLong(16)` fails above `Long.MAX_VALUE`.
A `clone` without `CLONE_THREAD` creates a process (that is what `fork()` does), so it is not a thread. One test feeds you such a line from a tiny shell.
`Regex("\"([^\"]*)\"").find(args)` finds the first quoted string, which is the path in an `openat` call.

drill.title: The trap, from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. Write down, in order, what happens from the moment your code calls `write(1, buf, 3)` until it gets 3 back. Name the CPU mode at each step and the arm64 register that holds the system call number. Then compare with the answer.

answer.src:
1. user mode (EL0): your code calls libc write(), an ordinary function call
2. user mode: the wrapper puts 64 (write) in x8 and the arguments in x0, x1, x2
3. svc #0 traps: the CPU saves the user PC, switches EL0 -> EL1 and jumps
   to the kernel's exception vector
4. kernel mode (EL1): look up entry 64 in the syscall table, run the write
   handler, check fd 1, copy 3 bytes from user memory
5. kernel mode: put the result in x0 (3, or a negative errno such as -9)
6. eret: back to EL0 at the instruction after svc
7. user mode: the wrapper returns 3 (or returns -1 and sets errno)

recap: Your code runs in user mode. Only the kernel, in kernel mode, can touch devices, memory maps and other processes.
A system call is a numbered request to the kernel. On arm64 the number goes in `x8`, the arguments in `x0` to `x5`, `svc #0` traps into the kernel and `eret` comes back.
Errors come back as negative numbers. libc turns them into -1 plus `errno`, and strace prints `= -1 ENOENT (...)`.
A JVM hello world makes about 1,400 system calls and starts 20 threads before `main` returns. Trace a JVM with `strace -f`, or you only watch the idle launcher thread.
The vDSO answers clock reads in user mode, about 17 ns against about 150 ns for a trap, and strace never sees those calls.
seccomp filters system calls on the way in. Docker's default profile answers `clone3` with `ENOSYS`, so glibc falls back to `clone`.

quiz.q: A payment service logs every authorization through an appender that calls `write` once per line, with no buffer. At 20,000 lines a second, which change cuts the number of system calls the most?
options: Switch the log format from JSON to plain text
Buffer lines in memory and write them 8 KB at a time
Log to standard error instead of standard output
Give the pod more CPU cores
quiz.why: Each `write` is one trap, whatever it carries. Buffering 100 lines into one `write` cuts the traps 100 times. A shorter format sends fewer bytes through the same number of calls. Standard error is just file descriptor 2, so the count stays the same. More cores don't change how many calls the code makes.

quiz.q: You run `strace -f -c` on a program that calls `System.currentTimeMillis()` five million times. The summary shows `clock_gettime` 4 times. What is the best explanation?
options: strace dropped events because the program ran too fast
The JIT compiler removed the calls
The clock reads go through the vDSO and never enter the kernel
`currentTimeMillis` caches the time and refreshes it 4 times
quiz.why: The C library answers `clock_gettime` from the vDSO, in user mode, so the kernel never sees those reads and strace can't count them. strace doesn't drop calls: it stops the program at each one. The JIT can't remove a call whose result the program uses.

quiz.q: A service that starts fine shows `openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/ledger/override.yaml", O_RDONLY) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)` in its trace. What does that line most likely mean?
options: The service crashed while it read its config
The service looked for an optional file that isn't there, which is normal
The file system is corrupted
seccomp blocked the call
quiz.why: `ENOENT` means no such file. Programs probe for optional files all the time. The JVM's start-up alone has 23 `ENOENT` failures. A seccomp block in Docker shows up as `EPERM` or `ENOSYS`, not `ENOENT`.

quiz.q: What actually stops a user program from writing straight to the disk controller?
options: The CPU refuses privileged instructions in user mode, so only kernel code can drive the device
The file permissions on the device file in `/dev`
The JVM, which checks every native call
Nothing: using system calls is a convention that well-behaved programs follow
quiz.why: The CPU enforces it in hardware. In user mode (EL0 on arm64, ring 3 on x86-64) the privileged instructions and the device's memory are off limits, so a program has to ask the kernel. Permissions on `/dev` decide whether the kernel will open the device for you, which is still a system call.

quiz.q: In the lab box a JVM's trace shows `clone3(...) = -1 ENOSYS` followed by `clone(...) = 70`. In the privileged box, which has no seccomp filter, the same JVM shows `clone3(...) = 70`. Why?
options: The privileged box runs a newer kernel
The JVM notices the container and uses a different thread library
strace can't decode `clone3` inside Docker
Docker's seccomp profile answers `clone3` with `ENOSYS`, so glibc falls back to `clone`
quiz.why: Both boxes share one kernel, 6.12. Docker's default seccomp profile makes `clone3` look missing, because a seccomp filter can't read the flags `clone3` keeps in memory. glibc falls back to `clone` only when it sees `ENOSYS`, so threads still start.

flashcards.back: A numbered request from a user program to the kernel, such as `openat`, `write` or `clone`. The CPU traps into kernel mode to run it.
It traps: the CPU saves the user program counter, switches from EL0 (user) to EL1 (kernel) and jumps to the kernel's exception vector. The call number is in `x8`.

flashcards.front: How does a failed system call report its error?
flashcards.back: The kernel returns a negative errno, such as -2 for `ENOENT`. libc returns -1 and sets `errno`. strace prints `= -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)`.

flashcards.front: Why does `strace -p <jvm pid>` show one futex line and nothing else?
flashcards.back: Without `-f` it attaches only to the launcher thread, which waits for main. Use `strace -f -p <pid>`.
A small library the kernel maps into every process so calls like `clock_gettime` run in user mode with no trap. strace and seccomp never see those calls.

flashcards.front: Rough cost of a trap versus a vDSO call in the lab box?
flashcards.back: About 150 ns for a `getpid` system call, about 17 ns for a vDSO `clock_gettime`.

flashcards.front: What does Docker's default seccomp profile do to `clone3`?
flashcards.back: It answers `ENOSYS`, so glibc falls back to `clone`, whose flags the filter can check.

terms.plain: The one program that runs in kernel mode. It owns the hardware and every process's memory, and decides what runs next.
CPU settings. User mode (EL0 on arm64) refuses privileged instructions; kernel mode (EL1) allows them.
A numbered request a user program makes to the kernel, such as `openat`, `write`, `mmap` or `clone`.
The CPU's switch from user mode into the kernel at a fixed entry point, caused by `svc` on arm64 or `syscall` on x86-64.
The error code a failed call leaves behind, such as `ENOENT` (no such file) or `EAGAIN` (try again).
A tool that stops a program at each system call and prints the call, its arguments and its result.
A small library the kernel maps into every process so a few read-only calls, mainly clock reads, run without a trap.
A filter the kernel runs on every system call a process makes. It can allow a call, refuse it, or make it look missing.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate traced a staging pod with `strace -f -c` for ten seconds. It showed 300,000 `write` calls but almost no `clock_gettime`, even though the code reads the clock on every request. Explain both numbers in your own words, and say what you would change.
explain_back.answer: Every `write` is a system call: the CPU traps into kernel mode, the kernel does the work and returns, and that costs something like 150 ns each time. 300,000 writes in ten seconds means about one per log line, so the logger has no buffer. Buffering lines and writing a few kilobytes at a time would cut the count by 100 times or more. The clock reads are missing because `clock_gettime` goes through the vDSO, a small library the kernel maps into the process. It reads the time from a page the kernel keeps current, in user mode, without a trap. strace only sees calls that enter the kernel, so it never counts them. They are cheap, so I would leave them alone.

deeper.body:
Every container in the lab box runs behind a seccomp filter. You can see it in the process status file, and you can see it refuse a call:

```text
$ grep Seccomp /proc/self/status
Seccomp:	2
Seccomp_filters:	1
$ unshare --user --map-root-user whoami
unshare: unshare failed: Operation not permitted
$ strace -f -e trace=unshare unshare --user --map-root-user whoami
unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER)                  = -1 EPERM (Operation not permitted)
```

`Seccomp: 2` means filter mode. `unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER)` asks for a new user namespace, a building block of containers that lesson 12 of this track takes apart. Docker's default profile refuses it with `EPERM`. In `box-priv` the same command prints `root` and the status file says `Seccomp: 0`.

Docker's documentation says its default profile disables around 44 system calls out of more than 300. Most are calls a normal program never needs: loading kernel modules, changing the clock, rebooting, `bpf`, `mount`. The profile also hides the three `io_uring` calls, which lesson 11 of this track comes back to. All containers on a host share one kernel, so a kernel bug reachable from one container is a bug for every container. Fewer reachable calls means fewer chances.

A seccomp filter is a small BPF program the kernel runs at the trap, before the system call table. It sees the call number, the architecture, the instruction pointer and the six argument registers, and nothing else. It can't follow a pointer, which is why it can't read `clone3`'s flags or the path given to `openat`. That is also why seccomp is good for "this program never needs `mount`" and useless for "this program may only open files under `/data`". Path rules need a different mechanism, such as AppArmor or SELinux.

One more number from this lesson to keep: the static C hello world made 14 system calls and the dynamic one 28. Half the work of a tiny dynamic program is the loader finding and mapping `libc.so.6`. For a JVM the loader's work is a rounding error next to `libjvm.so` building the heap and its threads.
